title: Decide where a catch-up answer carries its sequences: one header cannot, and decision mimid-1wgh.104 assumed one fanout per request
design:
Found 2026-11-25 starting bead mimid-1wgh.37.104.3. It blocks the wire
half of that bead; its store half (fanout_window) is done and does not
depend on this.

THE TENSION. Decision mimid-1wgh.104 put the fanout sequence BESIDE the
message rather than inside FanoutMessage, and bead mimid-1wgh.37.104.1
implemented that as the mimi-fanout-sequence header on
POST /notify/{roomId}. That works because a notify carries exactly one
fanout: the hub writes one outbox row per (event, destination) and sends
one row per request. I recorded that as a reason the choice was easy.

A CATCH-UP ANSWER CARRIES MANY FANOUTS (§5: "fanouts in hub order, each
with its sequence"). One header cannot say which sequence belongs to
which message, so the decision does not carry over, and this is the
first place .104's wording has to be extended rather than applied.

THE READINGS:

1. A WRAPPER, in the catch-up answer only. The sequence goes inside the
   answer's own structure, one per fanout.
   Against: the sequence then lives in two different places depending
   on the operation, which a reviewer of the protocol-08 text would
   question, and a catch-up answer stops being simply a concatenation
   of what was originally delivered.

2. AN RFC 8941 LIST HEADER, paralleling the body order:
   mimi-fanout-sequence: 41, 42, 43, with the body the same
   concatenated FanoutMessages a notify carries.
   For: .104 stays literally true in both operations; the answer is
   byte-identical to what was fanned out, which is the same property
   bead mimid-1wgh.37.104.2's ranges give (catch-up can only return what
   was really sent); and one rule covers both operations in the draft.
   Against: the pairing is positional, so a reordering or a dropped
   message misaligns it. Though both are covered together -- the RFC
   9421 signature covers the header and content-digest covers the body
   -- so a misalignment is a signature failure, not silent.

3. REVISIT .104 and put the sequence inside FanoutMessage after all,
   which is reading (1) of design note §4 that .104 rejected. Both
   operations then become trivial and no header is needed.
   Against: exactly the wire change to a struct other implementations
   already parse that .104 chose (2) to avoid. But it is worth
   re-asking now that we know (2) needs an extension anyway, because
   .104 was decided on the assumption that "beside the message" was
   free.

MY READ, and it is not a decision: reading 2. It keeps .104 true in
both operations, keeps a catch-up answer byte-identical to what was
delivered, and the positional worry is answered by the signature
covering header and body together. But this is wire format Mark will
propose as protocol-08 text (decision mimid-1wgh.105), so the choice is
his and not mine.

WHAT IS NOT BLOCKED by this: the store half of mimid-1wgh.37.104.3.
Store::fanout_window gives the oldest sequence still held and the
highest assigned, which is what §5.1's distinct out-of-window answer
rests on, and Store::serves (bead mimid-1wgh.37.104.2) gives the §8
bound. Both are in and tested. What waits is the route, the directory
template and the body format -- and the template must NOT be published
before the operation works, since §5 makes publishing it the whole of
the capability negotiation.
notes:
DECIDED by Mark 2026-11-25: inside the catch-up answer, one sequence
beside each message. Reading 1.

So the answer carries its own structure -- the hub's highest sequence,
then entries of (sequence, FanoutMessage) -- and no header. The
mimi-fanout-sequence header stays exactly as it is on
POST /notify/{roomId}, where one request is one fanout and the header is
right.

WHY, and the reasons corrected my own first read, which favoured a list
header:

* Decision mimid-1wgh.104's reasons are about not changing structures
  OTHER IMPLEMENTATIONS ALREADY PARSE: FanoutMessage and the /notify
  body. A catch-up answer is new and nothing parses it, so there is
  nothing to protect by keeping the sequence outside it. Reading 1
  contradicts .104's wording and none of its reasons.
* THE ARGUMENT I GAVE FOR A LIST HEADER WAS WRONG. I said positional
  misalignment would be caught because the RFC 9421 signature covers
  the header and content-digest covers the body. mimid signs REQUESTS
  ONLY and never responses (httpsig.rs limitations). A catch-up answer
  is unsigned, so a dropped or reordered message would misalign every
  later number with nothing to detect it.
* A 256-entry list header is about 1.8 KB, close to common per-header
  proxy caps, and would break if the limit rose. mimid asks for 256
  (design note §5).

NOT chosen: putting the sequence inside FanoutMessage (reading 3),
which would make both operations trivial. It was worth re-asking,
because .104 was decided partly on the assumption that "beside the
message" was free and catch-up shows it is not -- but reading 1 extends
.104 without paying the cost .104 declined.

Unblocks the wire half of bead mimid-1wgh.37.104.3.
